# How often are estimators defined?

```{r, include=FALSE}

# Calculate what proportion of time each estimator is defined ----
names(combined)
filter( combined, Estimator == "MLM-FE", Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Collection, UniqueID, ATE_hat_std, SE_hat_std ) %>%
  knitr::kable()

tallys <- combined %>%
  mutate( Covariates = factor( Covariates, levels = c( "none", "best", "all" ) ) ) %>%
  group_by( Estimator, Covariates, Project ) %>%
  summarise( na_ATE = mean( is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ),
             na_SE = mean( is.na( SE_hat_std ) ),
             n = n(), .groups = "drop" )

tallys %>%
  dplyr::filter( Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  knitr::kable()

# Which sets are fully defined?
tallys %>%
  dplyr::filter( Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  group_by( Project ) %>%
  summarise( na_ATE = max( na_ATE ),
             na_SE = max( na_SE ) ) %>%
  arrange( na_SE )

table( tallys$na_ATE )
table( tallys$na_SE )

tallys <- tallys %>%
  group_by( Estimator, Covariates ) %>%
  summarise( na_ATE = mean( na_ATE ),
             na_SE = mean( na_SE ),
             outs = sum( n ),
             n = n(), .groups = "drop" )

stopifnot( all( tallys$n == tallys$n[[1]] ) )

tallys$n
```

This is across `r tallys$outs[[1]]` outcomes.  Each column shows the percent of time the listed estimator is not defined when using the given covariate set. To calculate, I first averaged across the outcomes within a set, and then equally weighted these outcomes across sets.  For most datasets, either all the outcomes or none of the outcomes were defined for a given model.

```{r}
tallys %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from = Covariates, values_from = c(na_ATE, na_SE),
               names_vary = "fastest") %>%
  dplyr::select( -n, -outs, -na_ATE_none ) %>%
  arrange( -na_SE_all, -na_SE_best ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```


# What predicts larger or smaller estimated standard errors?

We run a regression of the log of the estimated standard error on the estimator, the type of estimator, degrees of freedom, sample size, and the covariate option used in the estimation. 

We restrict our attention to only those outcomes where all estimators have defined estimated standard errors for a given level of covariate adjustment.

```{r, include=FALSE }
library( lme4 )

source( here::here( "empirical/make_estimator_feature_table.R" ) )
combined <- left_join( combined, est_profile, by = "Estimator" )

combined$Covariates = factor( combined$Covariates, levels = c( "none", "best", "all" ) )

combined$log_SE = log( combined$SE_hat_std )
summary( combined$log_SE )
qplot( combined$log_SE )

cc <- combined %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, Covariates ) %>%
  mutate( num_na = sum( is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter( num_na == 0 )
nrow( cc )
nrow( combined )

summary( cc$log_SE )
qplot( cc$log_SE )

n_unique <- length( unique( combined$UniqueID ) )
nrow( combined ) / n_unique
n_unique_sub <- length( unique( cc$UniqueID ) )
table( cc$UniqueID, cc$Covariates )
nrow( cc ) / n_unique_sub
```

This subsetting takes us from `r length( unique( combined$UniqueID ) )` outcomes to `r length( unique( cc$UniqueID ) )` outcomes.  It also removes some extreme outliers of the estimated standard errors.

Our regression model is of the form:
```{r, echo=TRUE}
Msimp <- lmer( log_SE ~ Covariates + 
                 df + J + nbar + I(n/100) + I(100*cluster_ICC) + I(100*block_ICC) +
                 (1|UniqueID) + (1|UniqueID:Covariates) + (1|Estimator), 
               data = cc )
M <- update( Msimp, . ~ . +  Estimand + type + FI + db + crve )
```

We fit one model with just random effects for the estimators, and another with aspects of the estimators to see if certain qualities are associated with higher or lower estimated standard errors.

And the results are, when fit to all our estimates:
```{r}
make_table <- function( M ) {
  tidy( M ) %>%
    dplyr::filter( is.na( group ) ) %>%
    dplyr::select( -effect, -group ) %>%
    mutate(     est = exp( estimate ),
                CIl = exp( estimate - 2 * std.error ),
                CIh = exp( estimate + 2 * std.error ) ) %>%
    rename( log_est = estimate ) %>%
    relocate( term, est, CIl, CIh )
}
tt <- make_table( M )
tt %>% knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

I exponentiated all the coefficients so they are multiplicative factors.  A factor of 1.1 means a 10% increase over baseline, and a 0.9 means a 10% decrease.


```{r, include=FALSE}
R2 <- round( 100 * (1 - var( residuals( M ) ) / var( cc$log_SE ) ) )
R2

# Look at R2 of our model, alternate calculation
exp( fixef( M ) )

cc$pd = predict( M )

var( cc$pd ) / var( cc$log_SE )
```

Generally covariates reduce standard errors by 20% on average. Some of the estimators are systematically smaller (the crve estimators, for example).


The model explains `r R2`% of the variance in the log of the estimated standard errors.

We can also see if some estimators are systematically more varying than others:

```{r, include=FALSE}
R2 <- round( 100 * (1 - var( residuals( Msimp ) ) / var( cc$log_SE ) ) )
R2

ests <- ranef( Msimp )$Estimator %>%
  mutate( est = exp( `(Intercept)` ) ) %>%
  rownames_to_column( var = "Estimator" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( -`(Intercept)` )

cc$resid = residuals( M )
sd_base = sd( cc$resid )
esres <- cc %>%
  group_by( Estimator ) %>%
  summarise( sd_resid = sd( resid ) / sd_base,
             mean_resid = mean( resid ) ) 
esres
ests <- left_join( ests, esres, by = "Estimator" )
max( ests$est ) / min( ests$est )
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
ggplot( ests, aes( est ) ) +
  geom_dotplot( binwidth = 0.005) +
  scale_x_continuous( labels = scales::percent_format() )

ests %>%
  dplyr::select( Estimator, est, sd_resid ) %>%
  arrange( desc( est ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```

Overall, the estimated standard errors across estimators are, on average, about the same.  The highest is about 15% larger than the lowest, averaged across all the outcomes.

We can also look at whether the estimators have different residuals, which would give a sense of stability.
That is the third column on the table above.
In this column I calculated the ratio of the standard deviation of the residuals (in log space) divided by the overall standard deviation of the residuals.
This is both a measure of the instability of the estimator and also a measure of how well the model fits the data for that estimator, so it is unclear how reliable these numbers are.
That said, some estimators have much wider ranges of residuals than others.


# Looking at all the standard errors

We can plot all the standard errors to look at grouping.  We do this for the 'best' covariate set.

```{r, include=FALSE }
cc_best = subset( cc, Covariates == "best" )
qplot( cc_best$log_SE )
table( cc_best$FI )
```

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
ggplot( cc_best, aes( UniqueID, exp( log_SE ), col=type, 
                      pch=as.factor(FI) ) ) +
  geom_jitter( width = 0.15, alpha=0.7 ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( x = "", y = "Estimated Standard Error", pch = "FI estimator?", color = "Estimator type" )
```

We then replicate the regression from above, but just for the "best" covariate set.
```{r, include=FALSE}
Mbest <- update( M, . ~ . - Covariates - (1|UniqueID:Covariates), data = cc_best )
arm::display( Mbest )
exp( fixef( Mbest ) )

cc_best$pd = predict( Mbest )

var( cc_best$pd ) / var( cc_best$log_SE )

Msimple <- update( Mbest, . ~ . - type - crve  )
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
screenreg( list( core = Msimp, all = M, best_only = Mbest, simple = Msimple ) )
```

A regression table of the four regressions considered is as follows, with the point estimates exponentiated for interpretation:
```{r}
tabs <- bind_rows( core = make_table( Msimp ),
                   all = make_table( M ),
                   best = make_table( Mbest ), 
                   simple = make_table( Msimple ), .id = "model" )
tabs %>% 
  dplyr::select( model, term, est ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from = model, values_from = est ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2, na = "" )
```
